Antigen-processing machinery (APM) is the set of proteins that generate, transport and load peptides onto HLA. A common class I route has five steps. (1) The proteasome cuts intracellular proteins into fragments, which can create a useful peptide or destroy it. (2) The transporter associated with antigen processing, TAP1 with TAP2, moves peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum; Shepherd et al. (1993) showed in a cell-free system that TAP1 is part of an ATP-dependent, sequence-selective peptide translocator. (3) ERAP1 and ERAP2 trim amino acids from the front end. York et al. (2002) found that ERAP1 can enhance or limit presentation by trimming epitopes to 8 to 9 residues, and Saveanu et al. (2005) found complementary human ERAP1 and ERAP2 activity, so more expression does not universally improve display. A class I HLA heavy chain assembles with beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a peptide, with helpers such as tapasin. (4) Stable peptide-HLA complexes reach the surface; the peptide stays held by HLA. (5) A compatible T-cell receptor on a conventional CD8 T cell may recognise the pair; recognition is a separate gate and display alone does not show killing.

A computational study of spacer design for class-I-restricted string-of-beads polypeptides reported a fivefold increase in predicted epitope recovery and a 44 per cent reduction in predicted neo-epitope immunogenicity compared with designs without spacers (Schubert and Kohlbacher); these are predictions, not measured protection. Combining an N-terminal leader peptide with an MHC class I trafficking signal at the C terminus improved presentation of class I and class II epitopes in human and mouse dendritic cells and expanded antigen-specific CD8 and CD4 T cells in vitro and in mice (Kreiter and colleagues). In a first-in-human RNA poly-neo-epitope melanoma study all patients developed T-cell responses against multiple vaccine neo-epitopes (Sahin and colleagues; abstract only), and each patient's vaccine in the Rojas pancreatic cancer trial used two uridine mRNA strands, each encoding up to 10 neoepitopes. Mass spectrometry can identify recovered HLA-bound peptides. Caron and colleagues' 2015 review describes class I peptides predominantly 9 to 12 amino acids long and reports that about 10 per cent of acquired spectra could be confidently assigned at a 1 per cent false discovery rate in the workflows discussed. It also describes evidence that mass spectrometry underestimates the self-HLA peptide repertoire, so non-detection does not prove absence. Prediction is not presentation: of more than 1,300 amino acid changes in two mouse tumour models about 13 per cent were predicted to bind MHC class I and a small fraction of those were confirmed by mass spectrometry (Yadav and colleagues). Because a single amino acid after an epitope changed its immunogenicity in a multiepitope DNA vaccine (Livingston and colleagues, already linked), a changed spacer is a changed construct that needs renewed processing and display evidence, while earlier evidence is retained for the parts that did not change.

references.excerpt: RNA carries negative charge, and positively charged lipid components can associate with it. RNA-lipoplex names a family of formulations, and the final particle need not be positively charged: net charge depends on the balance of RNA and lipid, the ingredients and the preparation. The format changes what is made and what still needs to be tested. Solid-phase peptide synthesis assembles an amino-acid chain on a support, then releases and purifies it; antigen-presenting-cell loading or processing and priming remain biological questions. RNA supplies instructions, whether delivered in a specified nanoparticle or lipoplex. DNA and engineered vectors raise their own questions about expressing cells, duration and vector-specific risks. LNP and lipoplex labels can overlap in papers, so inspect composition and architecture. Record composition, RNA amount and integrity, particle properties and relevant biological activity for the chosen formulation. A new formulation or route can change behaviour even with the same message. Identity, purity, integrity, relevant activity, stability and handling are separate attributes: residual DNA, proteins, incomplete RNA and double-stranded RNA are not one measurement, and a low double-stranded-RNA signal does not establish sterility.

It is a set of evidence questions, not a required experimental sequence. Receptor binding, cytokine release, cell killing, lot potency and clinical benefit are different observations. Method card, what it measures: binding of cells to a specified peptide held by a specified HLA allele, under the staining conditions. How: HLA molecules are assembled with the selected peptide and several copies are attached to a labelled scaffold (a tetramer is one format), cells are exposed and analysed, usually by flow cytometry, with viable-cell and gate selection. Input: blood or tissue cells, where staining uses a defined aliquot and compatibility with later living-cell assays depends on the preparation, and the reagent must match both peptide and allele. Thresholds: gate and positivity rules need background and reagent controls, and no universal percentage shows efficacy. Failure modes: nonspecific binding, weak binding, dead cells, a wrong or poorly formed reagent, chain differences or sampling loss. It cannot tell cytokine response, tumour-cell killing, healthy-tissue specificity or benefit.

Method card, what it measures: cells that secrete a chosen molecule, most often interferon gamma, under defined stimulation, counted as spots on an antibody-coated membrane. How: capture antibodies hold the released molecule near the cell, the cells are removed and detection reagents make localised spots visible. Input: viable cells, often PBMCs, allocated to the test. Prior culture expansion changes the measured population, and the cells are removed before the membrane spots are read. Output: spot-forming units per stated number of input cells, with background handling stated. Thresholds: response and quality rules fixed in advance for that assay and study, so one paper's positivity rule is not imported into another laboratory's report. Failure modes: high background, dead cells, weak stimulation, merged spots, inconsistent counting or failed controls. It cannot tell each receptor's target, natural tumour recognition, safety in healthy tissue or clinical benefit.

Method card, what it measures: whether specified effector cells cause death of specified target cells under controlled laboratory conditions, at a stated effector-to-target ratio and time. Readouts: flow cytometry that separates labelled targets from effectors and uses death-associated staining, release assays, or imaging over time. A fall in a metabolic or growth signal can reflect slowed growth and not death, so it needs validation as evidence of killing. Controls: target-only survival wells, effector identification and viability, a positive-control response, irrelevant or antigen-negative targets and suitable antigen or presentation perturbations, plus maximum release where relevant. Failure modes: high spontaneous death, mistaken target identity, aggregates, dye transfer, artificial loading, mismatched ratios or a readout that mainly measures growth.

Immunogenicity asks whether an intervention elicits an immune response; clinical efficacy asks what adding it changes in a defined clinical endpoint, population and comparison. An immune result can justify further investigation without settling whether adding the intervention improves outcomes. For a therapeutic cancer vaccine, antigen-stimulated secretion and recurrence over follow-up answer different questions. The immune result needs its specimen, stimulus, preparation, timing, controls and denominator. The clinical result needs the intervention components, comparator, outcome rule, starting clock, follow-up, missing-data handling, harms and uncertainty. A surrogate endpoint also needs evidence connecting it to clinical benefit in that setting. Comparing standard care plus vaccine with the same care without vaccine can address the addition. Randomisation strengthens attribution, while measurement quality and follow-up remain necessary. Even a clinical outcome difference does not identify the particular clone or immune mechanism that caused it. The FDA's 2018 endpoint guidance informs these general distinctions, rather than current regulatory or treatment advice.
